quiz: List the five RADIO steps in order: Requirements and Architecture come first. What do you decide right after the architecture, before the API?
Debounce waits for a quiet period before acting. How many calls happen during a quick burst of typing?
Responses can arrive in any order. Ask how you would stop wasted work and how you would know whether a response still matches the current input.
Picture new posts arriving at the top while a user is on page 2. What happens to an offset, and what does a cursor refer to instead?
Divide the viewport height by the row height, then add the overscan rows.
If the server rejects an optimistic change, the UI must not keep showing something false.
Moving content must be controllable by users who need more time. Think about what control is required.
Two phones can disagree about the time by seconds. Ask who could give every message one order that all clients accept.
Think about what happens when a server restarts and every client retries on the same schedule.
Unread count is the gap between the latest message number and the last one the user read.
A spreadsheet is a dependency graph. Think about what must change when one input changes.
A cell is processed only when its waiting count reaches zero. What kind of dependency shape would keep some counts above zero forever?
Time is short and an unfinished app cannot be demoed. Which choice gives you something that works if time runs out?
Pure functions take inputs and return outputs with no side effects. Think about testing them.
interview: Follow a structure like requirements, architecture, data model, interface and optimizations, and state trade-offs as you go.
Cover debouncing, cancelling stale requests, caching results, keyboard navigation and accessibility, and handling slow responses.
Explain how offsets shift when new items arrive, causing duplicates or skips, and how a cursor stays stable and scales.
Explain rendering only visible rows plus overscan with spacers, and downsides like find-in-page, accessibility and variable heights.
Explain updating the UI before the server answers, keeping a snapshot to roll back, and handling errors, races and retries.
Mention keyboard controls, a pause button, labels and live regions, respecting reduced motion, and lazy loading images.
Explain server sequence numbers, deduping by message id, buffering gaps, and fetching missed messages after reconnect.
Describe storing a last read position per conversation on the server, syncing it across devices, and computing the count from it.
Cover detecting drops, exponential back-off with jitter, resuming from the last sequence, and showing connection status.
Explain cells with formulas, a dependency graph, recomputing in topological order, and detecting cycles.
Talk about virtualizing rows and columns, and using canvas when DOM node counts get too high, noting accessibility trade-offs.
Describe clarifying requirements, planning state, building a thin working slice first, then adding features, edge cases and tests.
Cover a clear data model, ordering, optimistic moves with rollback, keyboard drag alternatives and screen reader announcements.
Explain gains in boilerplate and speed, and risks like wrong code you cannot explain, so you must review and understand everything.
